## Why this series exists

This five-part series is my own coding-first walkthrough of the agentic-AI design
patterns taught in DeepLearning.AI's *Agentic AI* short course (Andrew Ng). All the
underlying ideas — reflection, tool use, evaluation/error analysis, planning and
multi-agent systems — come from that course. What's different here: every example is
rebuilt from scratch around **image segmentation**, and specifically the kind of
segmentation I do daily on semiconductor inspection images (X-ray void detection, AOI,
USM). If you've never touched agentic AI *or* image segmentation, you should still be
able to follow every line — I define every piece of jargon the first time it shows up.

The five posts map one course concept onto one stage of a segmentation pipeline:

1. **Preprocessing** → Tool use (this post)
2. **Training** → Planning
3. **Postprocessing** → Reflection
4. **Error analysis** → Evaluations & error analysis (the most important post — save it)
5. **Multi-agent system** → Everything combined, with an error-analysis agent at the center

None of the code below copies the course's lab notebooks line-for-line — I used them as
a starting point, found gaps, and rebuilt the exercises around segmentation images
instead of the course's original (non-imaging) examples.

## The core idea: what is "tool use"?

A large language model (LLM) only outputs text. It cannot open a file, run a
calculation, or look at pixel values. **Tool use** (also called *function calling*)
closes that gap: you describe a handful of Python functions to the model — name,
parameters, and a plain-English description of what each one does — and the model is
allowed to say "I want to call `normalize_xray(image_path=...)`" instead of trying to
answer from its own knowledge. Your code actually executes the function, feeds the
result back to the model, and the model continues.

This is the single most important upgrade you can give an LLM, because it turns a
"knows things" system into a "does things" system.

## Why preprocessing is a natural first tool-use example

Preprocessing in an X-ray/AOI/USM pipeline is a small set of well-defined, deterministic
operations: percentile normalization, tiling, artifact/QC checks, format conversion.
That determinism is exactly what makes it a good *first* agent to build — you're not
yet asking the LLM to make judgment calls, only to **choose and sequence the right
deterministic tool** given a plain-English request like *"prepare this batch of 16-bit
TIFs for the void-detection model."*

## Two ways to give an LLM tools

The course shows two patterns; both are worth knowing because you'll use one or the
other (or both) depending on where you're working.

### A) Bring-your-own-loop, via an API key

You write plain Python functions, describe them as a JSON schema, and drive the
call/execute/respond loop yourself. This works with any OpenAI-compatible endpoint —
including a **local vLLM server**, which matters a lot for semiconductor imaging data
that usually can't leave the company network.

```python
from openai import OpenAI
import json
from pathlib import Path
import numpy as np
import tifffile

# --- the actual preprocessing tools -------------------------------------

def normalize_xray(image_path: str, low_pct: float = 2.0, high_pct: float = 98.0) -> str:
    """Percentile-normalize a 16-bit X-ray TIF to 8-bit using p2/p98 clipping.
    This is the domain rule for X-ray void images: never use min/max normalization,
    it is destroyed by a handful of hot pixels."""
    img = tifffile.imread(image_path)
    lo, hi = np.percentile(img, [low_pct, high_pct])
    clipped = np.clip(img, lo, hi)
    img8 = ((clipped - lo) / (hi - lo) * 255).astype(np.uint8)
    out_path = str(Path(image_path).with_suffix(".norm.png"))
    tifffile.imwrite(out_path, img8)
    return out_path

def tile_image(image_path: str, tile_size: int = 512, overlap: int = 64) -> str:
    """Split a large inspection image into overlapping tiles for model input."""
    img = tifffile.imread(image_path)
    h, w = img.shape[:2]
    n_tiles = ((h // (tile_size - overlap)) + 1) * ((w // (tile_size - overlap)) + 1)
    return f"Tiled {image_path} ({h}x{w}) into ~{n_tiles} tiles of {tile_size}px, {overlap}px overlap"

def check_saturation(image_path: str) -> str:
    """QC check: flag images where >1% of pixels are saturated (sensor clipping)."""
    img = tifffile.imread(image_path)
    max_val = np.iinfo(img.dtype).max if np.issubdtype(img.dtype, np.integer) else img.max()
    sat_frac = (img >= max_val).mean()
    return f"{sat_frac:.3%} pixels saturated" + (" -- FLAG FOR REVIEW" if sat_frac > 0.01 else " -- OK")

TOOLS = [normalize_xray, tile_image, check_saturation]

def to_schema(fn):
    """Turn a Python function + docstring into the JSON schema the API expects."""
    import inspect
    sig = inspect.signature(fn)
    params = {
        name: {"type": "string"} for name in sig.parameters
    }
    return {
        "type": "function",
        "function": {
            "name": fn.__name__,
            "description": fn.__doc__,
            "parameters": {"type": "object", "properties": params,
                            "required": [n for n, p in sig.parameters.items()
                                         if p.default is inspect.Parameter.empty]},
        },
    }

# Point this at ANY OpenAI-compatible endpoint. Two examples below.
client = OpenAI(
    base_url="http://localhost:8000/v1",   # your local Qwen3-Coder-30B-A3B on the GX10
    api_key="not-needed-for-local-vllm",
)
MODEL = "Qwen3-Coder-30B-A3B"

def run_agent(user_request: str):
    messages = [{"role": "user", "content": user_request}]
    tool_map = {fn.__name__: fn for fn in TOOLS}
    for _ in range(6):  # max_turns, same idea as the course's aisuite max_turns
        resp = client.chat.completions.create(
            model=MODEL, messages=messages,
            tools=[to_schema(fn) for fn in TOOLS],
        )
        msg = resp.choices[0].message
        if not msg.tool_calls:
            return msg.content
        messages.append(msg)
        for call in msg.tool_calls:
            args = json.loads(call.function.arguments)
            result = tool_map[call.function.name](**args)
            messages.append({"role": "tool", "tool_call_id": call.id,
                              "content": str(result)})
    return "max turns reached"

print(run_agent(
    "Check /data/void_lot42/img_003.tif for saturation, then normalize it and tile it."
))
```

A note on style: the course's lab used the `aisuite` library, which auto-generates the
JSON schema from your docstrings and handles the loop for you (`max_turns=...`). I
wrote the loop out by hand above so you can see exactly what `aisuite` — or LangChain,
or the raw OpenAI SDK's own tool-calling — is doing under the hood. Once you understand
this loop, feel free to use whichever wrapper you like.

### B) Copilot / MCP style

The second pattern from the course: instead of writing the call/execute loop yourself,
you expose your tools through an **MCP server** (Model Context Protocol) and let an
existing agentic coding tool — GitHub Copilot agent mode, Claude Code, Cursor — call
them. MCP exists to solve the "M tools × N agent apps" integration problem: you write
your preprocessing tools *once* as an MCP server, and any MCP-compatible client can use
them without you writing a custom loop per client.

```python
# mcp_server.py — expose the same three functions as an MCP server
from mcp.server.fastmcp import FastMCP

mcp = FastMCP("preprocessing-tools")

@mcp.tool()
def normalize_xray(image_path: str, low_pct: float = 2.0, high_pct: float = 98.0) -> str:
    """Percentile-normalize a 16-bit X-ray TIF to 8-bit using p2/p98 clipping."""
    ...  # same body as above

@mcp.tool()
def tile_image(image_path: str, tile_size: int = 512, overlap: int = 64) -> str:
    """Split a large inspection image into overlapping tiles."""
    ...

@mcp.tool()
def check_saturation(image_path: str) -> str:
    """QC check for sensor saturation."""
    ...

if __name__ == "__main__":
    mcp.run()  # register this server's path in Copilot's / Claude Code's MCP config
```

Register `mcp_server.py` in your editor's MCP settings, and now you can just *ask*
Copilot chat: *"normalize and tile all TIFs in this folder, flag anything saturated"* —
no Python loop needed on your side at all. This is the pattern I use for my own Hermes
Agent setup: `tools.py` holds the plain functions, `mcp_server.py` wraps them for
interactive Copilot-agent use, and a cron job calls `tools.py` directly for unattended
batch runs.

## Which model to actually use

For learning and cheap experimentation, you don't need a frontier model — tool-call
routing on three simple, well-described functions is an easy task for most current
open-weight models. As of mid-2026, reasonable **free** options include Qwen3 (Apache
2.0, strong at code and reliable structured/function-calling output), and several
zero-cost models exposed through OpenRouter's free tier (subsidized by their
providers — rate-limited, but fine for a blog-post-scale demo).

If you're following along and happen to have serious local hardware, I run
**Qwen3-Coder-30B-A3B** myself via vLLM on an NVIDIA GX10 (Grace-Blackwell GB10,
128GB unified memory) — it's an MoE model that only activates ~3B parameters per
token, so it's fast even on a single unified-memory box, and it's more than capable of
routing three preprocessing tools correctly. For production accuracy on harder,
judgment-heavy tool calls you'll want to test a frontier model and compare — but for
this exercise, a free or local model is genuinely enough.

## Try it yourself

1. Swap `normalize_xray`, `tile_image`, `check_saturation` for whatever three
   deterministic steps your own preprocessing pipeline actually needs.
2. Run the same request through both patterns (A and B above) and compare how much
   code each one required.
3. Break something on purpose — pass a request that needs a tool you haven't written
   ("rotate the image 90 degrees") — and watch the model either refuse or hallucinate
   a tool call. This is the "missing tool = capability ceiling" lesson from the course,
   and it's the cleanest way to feel why tool design matters.
